title: Traits: capability as a contract
summary: A trait names what a type can do; impls and derives provide it; bounds demand it.
lecture: A trait is an interface with teeth: `Display` means "can be shown to users", `Debug` means "can be dumped for developers", `Default` means "has an obvious empty value". Types opt in via impl blocks — or via #[derive(...)] when the implementation is mechanical.

Generic code asks for capabilities with bounds: `fn announce<T: Display>(items: &[T])`. The right bound is read off the body — if you write {item} in a format string, you need Display, not Debug, not Clone. Demand exactly what you use.
Prefer derive over hand-written impls when they'd do the same thing (Clippy's derivable_impls flags the manual version) — less code, same contract, and it updates itself when fields change.

example.caption: Derives grant contracts; bounds spend them.
